deep.reconstruction:
This page is a draft of the historical part (§1) of Riemann's Habilitationsschrift 'Über die Darstellbarkeit einer Function durch eine trigonometrische Reihe' (1854, published 1867). It summarizes Dirichlet's 1829 convergence proof for the Fourier series. The text runs almost word for word as in the published version.

(A) Dirichlet's two lemmas. Let phi be monotone (always decreasing or always increasing) on the interval of integration.
(1) If 0 < c <= pi/2, then I_n = int_0^c phi(beta) sin((2n+1)beta)/sin(beta) dbeta -> (pi/2) phi(0) as n -> oo. Here phi(0) is to be read as phi(+0).
(2) If 0 < b < c <= pi/2, then int_b^c phi(beta) sin((2n+1)beta)/sin(beta) dbeta -> 0.
The implicit normalisation (my addition) is int_0^{pi/2} sin((2n+1)beta)/sin(beta) dbeta = pi/2 for every n. This follows from sin((2n+1)beta)/sin(beta) = 1 + 2 sum_{k=1}^n cos(2k beta).

(B) Application to the partial sums. From the previous page, the n-th partial sum is S_n(x) = (1/2pi) int_{-pi}^{pi} f(alpha) sin((2n+1)(x-alpha)/2)/sin((x-alpha)/2) dalpha. The following substitution is implicit; it is mine.
- Put alpha = x + 2beta on [x, x+pi] and alpha = x - 2beta on [x-pi, x], so that dalpha = 2 dbeta.
- Using periodicity, S_n(x) = (1/pi) int_0^{pi/2} [f(x+2beta) + f(x-2beta)] sin((2n+1)beta)/sin(beta) dbeta.
- If f has only finitely many maxima and minima, [0, pi/2] splits into finitely many intervals on which f(x +/- 2beta) is monotone.
- Lemma (1) on the first piece gives (1/pi)(pi/2) f(x+0) = f(x+0)/2, and likewise f(x-0)/2. Lemma (2) sends all other pieces to 0.
- Hence S_n(x) -> (f(x+0) + f(x-0))/2.

(C) Conclusion as Riemann states it. Every 2pi-periodic f that (1) is integrable throughout, (2) has finitely many maxima and minima, and (3) takes the mean of the one-sided limits at jumps is represented by its trigonometric series.
- A function satisfying (1) and (2) but not (3) is not representable, since the series would converge to the mean at the jump.
- For functions violating (1) or (2), the question remains open.

(D) Right-column note. A function with only finitely many maxima and minima has, at every x, one-sided limits f(x+0) and f(x-0) (Dirichlet's notation, Dove's Repertorium der Physik 1, p. 170), or else it becomes infinite. Reason: it is eventually monotone on each side of x.

(E) Historical assessment.
- Dirichlet settled a question open since 1753 (D. Bernoulli / Euler), bringing to light the point where Euler erred.
- For all functions occurring in nature the question is settled.
- The excluded cases still merit study, first because they bear on the principles of the infinitesimal calculus, as Dirichlet himself remarked. The page breaks off here; the next page adds number theory as the second reason.
errors: Lemma (1) as written uses phi(0); for a monotone function it must be the limit phi(+0). Boundedness of phi is also tacitly needed. This is standard looseness, not a real error.

The argument that a function violating condition 3 is 'obviously' not representable assumes something unproven. It takes for granted that any trigonometric series representing f off the jumps must be its Fourier series, i.e. uniqueness of trigonometric expansions. That was not established at the time (Cantor 1870 onward). Riemann's own later sections show awareness that general trigonometric series need not be Fourier series.

Condition 1 ('integrable throughout') goes beyond Dirichlet's 1829 hypotheses, which presuppose a bounded, piecewise monotone function. Dirichlet only remarked on extensions to unbounded functions. This is a paraphrase issue, not a mathematical error.

In the decomposition (my reconstruction), f(x+2beta) is monotone near beta = 0 only on a small initial interval [0, c]. The intervals must be chosen so that the first one starts at 0. Riemann's 'offenbar' covers this correctly.
